content.text: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance
2.1 Introduction

The notion of potential energy is not confined to mechanics alone. In electrostatics, work done in moving a charge in an electric field is stored as potential energy. This concept leads to the idea of electric potential.
Electric potential is analogous to gravitational potential. Just as a mass at height h has gravitational potential energy mgh, a charge in an electric field has electric potential energy qV.
This chapter deals with electric potential, potential energy, equipotential surfaces, capacitance, and the behaviour of capacitors with and without dielectrics.
2.2 Electrostatic Potential
Consider an electric field E⃗ due to a source charge. Work done in moving a test charge q₀ from point A to point B is independent of the path taken — the field is conservative.
W_{A \to B} = \int_{A}^{B} \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{l} = q_0 \int_{A}^{B} \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{l}
The electrostatic potential difference between points A and B is the work done per unit positive charge in moving a small test charge from A to B.
V_B - V_A = \int_{A}^{B} \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{l}
Potential is a scalar quantity with unit volt (V) = J C⁻¹. Potential at a point is the potential energy per unit charge at that point: V = U/q₀.
Choosing potential at infinity to be zero (V(∞) = 0), the potential at point P due to a charge q at distance r:
V(P) = \frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}
Potential due to positive charge is positive; due to negative charge is negative. Potential decreases along the direction of the electric field.
Electric potential is a scalar — it has magnitude and sign but no direction. This makes superposition simpler than for electric field (which is a vector).
2.3 Potential Due to a Point Charge
The potential at a distance r from a point charge q (taking V = 0 at infinity) is obtained by integrating the field along a radial path:
V(r) = \frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}
The potential varies as 1/r, while the field varies as 1/r². Both are positive for positive charges and negative for negative charges.
Work done in moving charge q₀ from A (r_A) to B (r_B) in the field of charge q:
W_{A \to B} = q_0 (V_B - V_A) = \frac{q q_0}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\frac{1}{r_B} - \frac{1}{r_A}\right)

props.title: Example 2.1 — Potential Due to a Point Charge

content.text:
A charge +2 μC is placed at the origin. Find potential at (0.3 m, 0).

V = q/(4πε₀r) = (2 × 10⁻⁶ × 9 × 10⁹)/0.3 = 6 × 10⁴ V

Work to bring 4 μC from infinity: W = q₀V = 4 × 10⁻⁶ × 6 × 10⁴ = 0.24 J

The work done is stored as potential energy of the system.
2.4 Potential Due to an Electric Dipole
For a dipole with moment p⃗ at the origin, the potential at a point P (r, θ) in polar coordinates (where θ is the angle between p⃗ and r̂) is:
V(r, \theta) = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{p \cos\theta}{r^2} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{\vec{p} \cdot \hat{r}}{r^2}
Potential varies as 1/r² (compared to 1/r for a point charge). It falls off faster because positive and negative charges partially cancel.
Along the equatorial plane (θ = 90°), V = 0 everywhere. The potential is maximum on the axial line at θ = 0° and minimum at θ = 180°.
The potential energy of a dipole p⃗ in an external field E⃗:
U = -\vec{p} \cdot \vec{E} = -pE \cos\theta

A dipole (p = 10⁻²⁹ C·m) is rotated from θ = 90° to θ = 0° in E = 10⁴ N/C.

ΔU = −pE cos 0° − (−pE cos 90°) = −pE = −10⁻²⁹ × 10⁴ = −10⁻²⁵ J

The negative sign indicates energy is released. Heat released = 10⁻²⁵ J.
2.5 Potential Due to a System of Charges
Superposition Principle for Potential: The potential at a point due to a system of charges is the algebraic sum of potentials due to individual charges.
V(P) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{q_i}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r_{iP}}
Since potential is a scalar, we simply add numbers — no vectors or components needed. This is a major advantage over computing electric field.
2.6 Equipotential Surfaces
An equipotential surface is a surface on which the potential is the same at every point. No work is done in moving a charge along an equipotential surface.

Properties of equipotential surfaces: (i) Electric field is perpendicular to the surface at every point. (ii) No work is done in moving a charge on the surface. (iii) Surfaces can never cross each other. (iv) They are closer together where the field is stronger.
For a point charge, equipotential surfaces are concentric spheres. For a uniform field, they are parallel planes. For a dipole, they are more complex but still perpendicular to field lines.
2.6.1 Relation between Field and Potential
The electric field component along any direction equals the negative rate of change of potential in that direction:
E_l = -\frac{\partial V}{\partial l}
In three dimensions, the electric field is the negative gradient of the potential:
\vec{E} = -\nabla V = -\frac{\partial V}{\partial x}\hat{i} - \frac{\partial V}{\partial y}\hat{j} - \frac{\partial V}{\partial z}\hat{k}
The potential difference between two points is the negative of the line integral of E⃗ along any path connecting them: V_B − V_A = −∫_A^B E⃗ · dl⃗.
2.7 Potential Energy of a System of Charges
The potential energy of a system of charges equals the work done in assembling the configuration — bringing each charge from infinity to its position, one at a time.
Potential energy of two charges q₁ and q₂ separated by distance r₁₂:
U = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{r_{12}}
For like charges, U > 0 (energy must be supplied to bring them together). For unlike charges, U < 0 (energy is released when they come together).
For a system of n charges, the total potential energy is the sum over all pairs:
U = \sum_{i < j} \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q_i q_j}{r_{ij}}

Two charges 1 μC and −2 μC are 0.5 m apart.

U = (1/4πε₀)(q₁q₂/r) = (9 × 10⁹)(1 × 10⁻⁶)(−2 × 10⁻⁶)/0.5 = −3.6 × 10⁻² J

The negative sign means energy is released when the system is assembled from infinity.
2.8 Potential Energy in an External Field
When charges are placed in an external field (produced by other charges), the potential energy depends on the interaction with that field and the mutual interaction between the charges.
2.8.1 Potential Energy of a Single Charge
For a charge q in external potential V(r⃗) at position r⃗:
U = qV(\vec{r})
Work done in displacing the charge from r⃗_A to r⃗_B:
W = q[V(\vec{r}_B) - V(\vec{r}_A)]
2.8.2 Potential Energy of a System of Two Charges
For two charges q₁ at r⃗₁ and q₂ at r⃗₂ in an external field:
U = q_1 V(\vec{r}_1) + q_2 V(\vec{r}_2) + \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{r_{12}}
The first two terms are interactions with the external field; the last term is the mutual interaction.
2.8.3 Potential Energy of a Dipole in an External Field
For a dipole p⃗ at position r⃗ in external field E⃗:
U = -\vec{p} \cdot \vec{E}
Minimum energy (U = −pE) occurs when p⃗ is aligned with E⃗ (θ = 0°). Maximum energy (U = +pE) occurs when p⃗ is anti-aligned (θ = 180°).
2.9 Electrostatics of Conductors
Conductors contain free electrons that move in response to an electric field. In electrostatics (charges at rest), conductors have unique properties.

Six properties of conductors in electrostatic equilibrium:
(i) The interior field is zero at all points.
(ii) The net charge in the interior is zero.
(iii) Any excess charge resides on the surface.
(iv) The electric field at the surface is perpendicular to the surface.
(v) The surface is an equipotential.
(vi) The field just outside is E = σ/ε₀, directed along the outward normal.
The field inside is zero because if there were a component along the conductor, it would drive free charges into motion, contradicting the assumption of electrostatic equilibrium.
For a charged conductor with surface charge density σ, applying Gauss's Law to a small pillbox at the surface:
E_{\text{surface}} = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} \hat{n}
The surface charge density (and hence the field) is greatest where the radius of curvature is smallest — at sharp points and edges. This is why lightning rods have pointed tips.
2.10 Dielectrics and Polarisation
Dielectrics are insulating materials that can be polarised by an external field. Unlike conductors, they have no free charges, but their molecular charge distributions can shift.
Polarisation P⃗ is the dipole moment per unit volume induced in a dielectric by an external field.
\vec{P} = \varepsilon_0 \chi_e \vec{E}
Here χ_e is the electric susceptibility of the material — a dimensionless quantity that measures how easily the dielectric polarises. For vacuum, χ_e = 0.
In polar molecules (like H₂O), permanent dipoles align with the field. In non-polar molecules (like N₂), the field induces a dipole by displacing the electron cloud relative to the nucleus.
The induced surface charges on the dielectric create a field opposite to the external field, reducing the net field inside.
Dielectrics reduce the field inside by a factor of K (dielectric constant). The reduced field is E = E₀/K, where E₀ is the field without the dielectric.
2.11 Capacitors and Capacitance
A capacitor is a device that stores electric charge and energy. It consists of two conductors separated by an insulator (vacuum or dielectric).
Capacitance C is defined as the ratio of the magnitude of charge Q on either conductor to the magnitude of potential difference V between them.
C = \frac{Q}{V}
Capacitance is a geometric property — it depends only on the shape, size, and separation of conductors and the dielectric between them. It does not depend on Q or V.
Unit of capacitance: farad (F) = C V⁻¹. In practice, capacitors are in μF, nF, or pF range. The SI unit F is very large.
2.12 The Parallel Plate Capacitor
Two parallel conducting plates of area A, separated by distance d, with equal and opposite charges ±Q. The field between the plates is uniform (neglecting edge effects).
E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} = \frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0 A}
The potential difference between the plates:
V = Ed = \frac{Qd}{\varepsilon_0 A}
Therefore the capacitance:
C_0 = \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}
Capacitance increases with plate area and decreases with separation. Edge effects become significant when d is comparable to the plate dimensions.
2.13 Effect of Dielectric on Capacitance
When a dielectric of dielectric constant K fills the space between the plates, the field is reduced by factor K, the potential difference is reduced, and the capacitance increases.
C = KC_0 = \frac{K\varepsilon_0 A}{d}
The permittivity of the dielectric is ε = Kε₀. The dielectric constant K ≥ 1 (equals 1 for vacuum). K is also called relative permittivity.
If the capacitor is isolated (Q constant), inserting a dielectric reduces V and increases C. If connected to a battery (V constant), inserting a dielectric increases Q and C.

props.title: Example 2.8 — Dielectric Slab Partially Filling Capacitor

content.text:
A parallel plate capacitor with plates 0.15 m apart has a dielectric slab (K = 3) of thickness 0.03 m filling the space.

Effective separation: d_eff = d − t + t/K = 0.15 − 0.03 + 0.03/3 = 0.13 m

The capacitance increases because the effective air gap is reduced.
2.14 Combination of Capacitors
2.14.1 Capacitors in Series
In series, the same charge Q flows through each capacitor, but the potential differences add up.
\frac{1}{C_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2} + \cdots
The equivalent capacitance in series is always less than the smallest individual capacitance.
2.14.2 Capacitors in Parallel
In parallel, the potential difference V is the same across each capacitor, but the charges add up.
C_{\text{eq}} = C_1 + C_2 + \cdots
The equivalent capacitance in parallel is always greater than the largest individual capacitance.

Same charge Q on each capacitor
Voltages add: V = V₁ + V₂ + ...
1/C_eq = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ + ...
Equivalent C < smallest C
Used when higher voltage needed

Same voltage V across each capacitor
Charges add: Q = Q₁ + Q₂ + ...
C_eq = C₁ + C₂ + ...
Equivalent C > largest C
Used when higher charge storage needed

Four capacitors (2 μF, 4 μF, 6 μF, 8 μF) arranged in a network.

Identify series and parallel groups, then calculate equivalent capacitance step by step.

For series: 1/C_s = 1/2 + 1/4 = 3/4, so C_s = 4/3 μF
For parallel with 6 μF: C_p = 4/3 + 6 = 22/3 μF
2.15 Energy Stored in a Capacitor
Energy is stored in a capacitor because work must be done to separate charges. The work done in charging a capacitor from 0 to Q is stored as electric potential energy.
U = \frac{1}{2}QV = \frac{1}{2}CV^2 = \frac{Q^2}{2C}
These three expressions are equivalent (using Q = CV). The energy is distributed throughout the field between the plates.
The energy density (energy per unit volume) in an electric field:
u = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2
This formula applies to any electric field, not just between capacitor plates. The total energy is obtained by integrating the energy density over the volume.

When a charged capacitor is disconnected from the battery, Q remains constant. When connected to the battery, V remains constant. The stored energy changes differently in each case when a dielectric is inserted.

props.title: Example 2.10 — Capacitor Charging and Energy Sharing

content.text:
A 4 μF capacitor charged to 200 V is connected to an uncharged 6 μF capacitor.

Conservation of charge: Q = C₁V₁ = (4 × 10⁻⁶)(200) = 8 × 10⁻⁴ C
Common voltage: V = Q/(C₁ + C₂) = 8 × 10⁻⁴/(10 × 10⁻⁶) = 80 V

Energy before: ½(4 × 10⁻⁶)(200)² = 0.08 J
Energy after: ½(10 × 10⁻⁶)(80)² = 0.032 J

Energy lost = 0.048 J — dissipated as heat in connecting wires.

props.title: Example 2.2 — Zero Potential Point Between Two Charges

content.text:
Two charges +5 μC and −3 μC are 16 cm apart. Find points where V = 0.

Case 1: Between charges (x from +5 μC)
5/(x) = 3/(16−x) → 5(16−x) = 3x → x = 10 cm from +5 μC

Case 2: Outside (beyond −3 μC)
5/(16+x) = 3/x → 5x = 3(16+x) → x = 24 cm from −3 μC

Two points exist: 10 cm from +5 μC (between) and 24 cm from −3 μC (outside).

props.title: Example 2.3 — Field Lines and Potential Signs

content.text:
Two charges +q and −q form a dipole. Along the axial line, the field lines point from +q to −q. The potential is positive near +q, zero at the midpoint, and negative near −q.

Along the equatorial line, V = 0 everywhere, but the field is non-zero and directed opposite to p⃗.

props.title: Example 2.4 — Four Charges at Square Corners

content.text:
Four charges +q at corners of a square of side a. Find potential at centre.

Distance from each corner to centre = a/√2
V = 4 × q/(4πε₀(a/√2)) = 4√2 q/(4πε₀a) = √2 q/(πε₀a)

The potential is scalar, so we add four equal contributions.
Summary
The electrostatic potential difference between two points is the work done per unit positive charge in moving a small test charge between them.
Potential due to a point charge: V = q/(4πε₀r). It is a scalar quantity.
Potential due to a dipole: V = (1/4πε₀)(p cos θ)/r². Zero on equatorial plane.
Superposition for potential: V = Σ q_i/(4πε₀ r_i). Scalar addition — no vectors needed.
Equipotential surfaces have E⃗ perpendicular to them. No work is done moving charge along them.
Field-potential relation: E⃗ = −∇V. Electric field is the negative gradient of potential.
PE of two charges: U = q₁q₂/(4πε₀ r₁₂). Total PE is sum over all pairs.
PE of dipole in external field: U = −p⃗ · E⃗. Minimum when aligned with field.
Conductors in electrostatic equilibrium: E = 0 inside, excess charge on surface, surface is equipotential, E = σ/ε₀ at surface.
Polarisation P⃗ = ε₀ χ_e E⃗. Dielectrics reduce field by factor K (dielectric constant ≥ 1).
Capacitance C = Q/V. For parallel plate: C₀ = ε₀A/d (vacuum), C = KC₀ (with dielectric).
Series: 1/C_eq = Σ 1/Cᵢ. Parallel: C_eq = Σ Cᵢ.
Stored energy: U = ½QV = ½CV² = Q²/2C. Energy density: u = ½ε₀E².
Points to Ponder
Potential is defined only for conservative fields (electrostatic fields). For non-conservative fields, potential difference depends on the path.
The potential due to a dipole falls as 1/r², while for a point charge it falls as 1/r. For a quadrupole, it falls as 1/r³.
Equipotential surfaces and field lines are perpendicular. Where field lines are dense, equipotential surfaces are closely spaced.
Inside a conductor, E = 0 in electrostatics. The field is discontinuous at the surface — it jumps from 0 to σ/ε₀.
Dielectrics are characterised by K ≥ 1. For metals (conductors), K → ∞. This is why E = 0 inside a conductor.
The energy stored in a capacitor resides in the electric field between the plates, not on the plates themselves.
When a dielectric is inserted into an isolated capacitor, energy decreases (work done by field on dielectric). When connected to a battery, energy increases (battery does work).
The capacitance of a conductor depends on its shape, size, and surrounding medium — not on the charge or potential.
